text:
Plutarch's essay on "whether 'Live Unknown' is a wise precept" (from Moralia) is the best framework on how to think about your relationship with the world:

--

"For my part I should say, Even if your life be bad do not live unknown, but be known, reform, repent; if you have virtue, be not utterly useless in life; if you are vicious, do not continue unreformed."

"Our remote ancestors paid public attention to the sick, and if any one had either had or cured a similar complaint, he communicated his experience to the patient, and so they say medical art became great by these contributions from experience. We ought also in the same way to expose to everyone diseased lives and the passions of the soul..."

"...But nowadays people deny and conceal and cloak their vices, and so fix them deeper in themselves."

--

for some of you, this puts words to how you already felt - or at least it did for me.

I doubt I can convince anyone on the opposite side, but it can't hurt to try.

1/4

you can either be public or you can be anonymous ("Live Unknown").

you gain everything in being public. whatever you contribute is (ideally) useful to others and to humanity as a whole. 

at the same time, you help yourself...whether that be testing ideas or using the world as a mirror to try and improve yourself for the better.

there really is no downside. you will be criticized and you will be judged. the same happened to every human worth a shit throughout history...I think you'll be okay. 

2/4

on the flipside, Plutarch views withdrawing into obscurity as self-defeating and cowardly on all fronts. 

hence the medical analogy he uses...progress depends on shared experience, as we look for symptoms and cures for the "diseases of the soul."

whether you are good or bad is completely irrelevant. if you are like every other human that has ever lived, some of you is good, and some of you is bad. let future generations sort that out. humanity will find a use for whatever you've got going on.

but in "Living Unknown," you are depriving everyone. depriving yourself from improving, and depriving the world of your example.

3/4

especially if you read and write a lot, you develop a strange sense of civic duty... where you feel that no matter how your life turns out, for good or for ill, you are obligated to document your experience and try to say something in a way that hasn't been said before.

or, at the same time, you can offer yourself up as a diseased carcass to be analyzed....Ben Franklin's "Either write something worth reading or do something worth writing."

and then, when u expire, u toss it all onto this flaming wretched heap we call humanity in hopes that you may advance the ball by even an inch.

you're basically a living organ donor, in a sense. don't take yourself too seriously. every one of us is just a microcosmic speck in this strange science experiment we've found ourselves in.

4/4

I'm hoping this helps change your worldview. worry less about what people think of you today and worry more about what they'll think of you 500 years from now. 

if you read a lot, you already know: posterity is the only audience that anyone great has ever focused on. 

so, what you do with this information is up to you. but I think in deciding to live life hidden, in the shadows, Plutarch is correct to be somewhat condemnatory...all you're doing is depriving yourself and your fellow man.

you have nothing to lose and everything to gain

do not Live Unknown, friend.
